items.rationale: The Windows appliance needs its own kernel, which only a VM supplies; the regulated workload needs the strongest boundary available, which is a VM's own kernel rather than a shared one; the frequently redeployed stateless service benefits from a container's start time and density, with no foreign-kernel or heightened-isolation requirement working against it. All three still sit on a type 1 hypervisor the provider operates, whether or not the workload itself is containerised.

items.stem: A team says 'containers are lightweight, so we should containerise everything and stop paying for virtual machines.' What mechanism does that slogan skip over?

options.text: The isolation cost — because containers share the host kernel, a kernel-level flaw has a blast radius covering every container on that host, which the slogan does not price in.
options.why: The guide is explicit that answering the container-versus-VM question needs the mechanism, not the slogan, and the isolation trade-off is exactly what 'lightweight' glosses over.

options.text: The mechanism it skips is that containers cannot run on shared physical hardware, unlike virtual machines; containers run on shared hardware routinely, and that density is the whole basis for the slogan; the actual gap is the isolation cost, not a hardware-sharing limitation.
options.why: Containers run on shared hardware routinely, and that density is the whole basis for the slogan; the actual gap is the isolation cost, not a hardware-sharing limitation.

options.text: It skips over the fact that containers are always more expensive per workload than virtual machines; containers typically cost less per workload precisely because the operating system overhead is shared rather than duplicated; this reverses the usual cost relationship.
options.why: Containers typically cost less per workload precisely because the operating system overhead is shared rather than duplicated; this reverses the usual cost relationship.

options.text: It skips over the fact that virtual machines cannot run on public cloud infrastructure at all; virtual machines are the canonical IaaS product on every public cloud platform; nothing about the container-versus-VM choice excludes VMs from cloud infrastructure.
options.why: Virtual machines are the canonical IaaS product on every public cloud platform; nothing about the container-versus-VM choice excludes VMs from cloud infrastructure.

items.rationale: 'Lightweight' describes density and start time honestly, but it says nothing about the isolation boundary being given up: because the kernel is shared, administrators must constrain memory and CPU so one container cannot starve the rest, and a kernel-level compromise is not contained the way it would be inside a VM's own kernel. Picking containers for everything trades that boundary away without pricing the trade.

items.stem: What does the named comparison 'container vs virtual machine' refer to, as distinct from the concept 'virtual machine' on its own?

options.text: It names the selection decision between two isolation technologies — which one to use for a given requirement — while 'virtual machine' names one of the two concrete things being selected between.
options.why: The comparison is a decision an engineer makes; a virtual machine is a thing an engineer creates, boots and destroys — different categories answering different questions.

options.text: They are the same concept under two names, since every virtual machine question is really a container-versus-VM question.
options.why: A question can ask purely 'what is a virtual machine' or 'who patches it' with no container involved at all; the comparison specifically concerns the choice between the two technologies.

options.text: The comparison names a specific orchestration tool used to run containers on top of virtual machines; no orchestration tool is implied by either term; the comparison is a conceptual selection decision, not a piece of named software.
options.why: No orchestration tool is implied by either term; the comparison is a conceptual selection decision, not a piece of named software.

options.text: The comparison applies only to on-premises infrastructure, while 'virtual machine' applies only to cloud infrastructure.
options.why: Neither term is restricted to one setting — virtual machines and the choice between them and containers both apply equally on-premises and in the cloud.

items.rationale: 'Container vs virtual machine' names the requirements-to-choice decision itself — an axis, not a thing you can create. 'Virtual machine' names one of the two concrete options inside that decision, the kind of entity a definition or responsibility-boundary question would ask about directly. The same relationship holds between any comparison and either of its members.

items.stem: Under AWS's stated shared responsibility model, which layer marks the boundary between what the provider controls and what the customer controls?

options.text: The host operating system and virtualization layer — the provider controls everything at and below that; the customer manages the guest OS, its patches, and their own application software.
options.why: This matches AWS's own stated boundary: provider from the host OS and virtualization layer down to physical security; customer from the guest OS upward.

options.text: The network perimeter — the provider secures everything outside the customer's virtual network, and the customer secures everything inside it.
options.why: The actual boundary is drawn at the operating system and virtualization layer, not at the network perimeter, and the provider-supplied firewall's configuration remains a customer duty regardless of network boundary.

options.text: The application layer — the provider is responsible for securing everything up to and including the customer's own application code.
options.why: This overstates the provider's share, especially under IaaS, where application software and its configuration remain the customer's responsibility.

options.text: The billing account — everything under one account is the provider's responsibility, and everything under a separate account is the customer's.
options.why: Account structure has nothing to do with the security responsibility boundary, which is defined by infrastructure layer, not by account organisation.

items.rationale: AWS states its own side as operating, managing and controlling everything from the host operating system and virtualization layer down to the physical security of the facilities, while the customer manages the guest operating system — including updates and security patches — other application software, and the configuration of the provider-supplied firewall. That single boundary is the one candidates most often misplace.

items.stem: A team moves an application from IaaS to a fully managed SaaS product from the same provider. What happens to the shared responsibility boundary?

options.text: It moves toward the provider — almost everything operational becomes the provider's, though the customer's own data and their identity and access configuration never transfer.
options.why: The guide states this directly: the lower the service model, the more the customer owns, and under SaaS almost everything operational moves to the provider — but data, identity and access remain the customer's at every level.

options.text: It disappears entirely, since SaaS providers assume full responsibility once a customer subscribes; no service model removes the customer's responsibility for their own data and for who they grant access to — the boundary moves, but it never vanishes.
options.why: No service model removes the customer's responsibility for their own data and for who they grant access to — the boundary moves, but it never vanishes.

options.text: It stays fixed, since the responsibility boundary is set once per provider account rather than per service model; AWS itself notes that responsibility varies by the specific services chosen; the boundary is per-service, and it visibly slides as the service model moves from IaaS toward SaaS.
options.why: AWS itself notes that responsibility varies by the specific services chosen; the boundary is per-service, and it visibly slides as the service model moves from IaaS toward SaaS.

options.text: It moves toward the customer, since SaaS applications expose more configuration surface than IaaS instances do; SaaS narrows, rather than widens, the customer's operational surface; configuration options are typically more limited than the full OS-and-application control IaaS provides.
options.why: SaaS narrows, rather than widens, the customer's operational surface; configuration options are typically more limited than the full OS-and-application control IaaS provides.

items.rationale: The model slides with the service model rather than staying fixed: under IaaS the customer patches the guest OS and owns application configuration, while under SaaS almost everything operational — patching, capacity, runtime — moves to the provider. What never moves at any service model is the customer's own data and their identity and access configuration, which is why moving to SaaS narrows but never eliminates customer responsibility.

items.stem: What is the structural relationship between a region and an availability zone?

options.text: An availability zone is one of multiple isolated locations inside a single region, each with independent power, cooling and networking.
options.why: This is exactly how the two nest: region is the broader geographic area, and zones are the isolated datacentre groupings within it.

options.text: A region is one of multiple availability zones grouped within a larger datacentre; this inverts the nesting — the region is the larger geographic container, and availability zones are the smaller isolated units inside it, not the reverse.
options.why: This inverts the nesting — the region is the larger geographic container, and availability zones are the smaller isolated units inside it, not the reverse.

options.text: Regions and availability zones are two names for the same unit of infrastructure; they are two distinct, nested units with different failure scopes: zones address one datacentre-scale failure, regions address the loss of a whole geography.
options.why: They are two distinct, nested units with different failure scopes: zones address one datacentre-scale failure, regions address the loss of a whole geography.

options.text: An availability zone spans multiple regions to provide cross-geography redundancy; an availability zone sits inside exactly one region; cross-geography redundancy is what spreading resources across separate regions provides instead.
options.why: An availability zone sits inside exactly one region; cross-geography redundancy is what spreading resources across separate regions provides instead.

items.rationale: A region is a separate geographic area designed to be isolated from other regions, and an availability zone is one of several isolated locations inside a single region, each with independent power, cooling and networking infrastructure — so that an outage in one zone is survived by the rest of the region.

items.stem: A service is deployed across three availability zones within one region for resilience. A regional-scale event takes out the entire region. Does the multi-AZ deployment protect against it?

options.text: No — availability zones protect against the failure of one datacentre-scale location within a region, not against the loss of the region itself.
options.why: The guide is explicit about the boundary: zones address one facility's failure; a whole-region event needs redundancy across separate regions instead.

options.text: Yes — spreading across multiple availability zones is sufficient protection against any scale of outage, including a whole-region event.
options.why: Multi-AZ redundancy is bounded by the region it sits inside; nothing about it survives an event that takes out the region as a whole.

options.text: Yes, because AWS automatically replicates all resources across regions by default; AWS states the opposite: resources are tied to the region specified and are not automatically replicated across regions unless a cross-region design is explicitly built.
options.why: AWS states the opposite: resources are tied to the region specified and are not automatically replicated across regions unless a cross-region design is explicitly built.

options.text: No, but only because the service should have used a hybrid cloud architecture instead of multiple zones; this hybrid cloud concerns mixing deployment models, not geographic redundancy; the actual gap here is the absence of a second region, which a hybrid architecture does not by itself supply.
options.why: Hybrid cloud concerns mixing deployment models, not geographic redundancy; the actual gap here is the absence of a second region, which a hybrid architecture does not by itself supply.

items.rationale: Availability zones are isolated datacentre groupings inside one region, so spreading a service across them protects against the loss of any single facility within that region. A regional-scale event is outside that protection boundary entirely; surviving it requires resources placed in a second region, which — because inter-region traffic is generally not fast enough for synchronous replication — is usually an asynchronous, more deliberate design decision.

items.stem: A team connects to a provider-operated relational database through its normal wire protocol, configuring schema, indexes and access grants, but deploying no application code onto the database itself. Is this PaaS, and what is the deciding fact?

options.text: No — it is a managed service; the deciding fact is whose code is running, and nothing of the team's is deployed onto the database.
options.why: The guide's separating axis is exactly this: PaaS runs an application the consumer wrote, while a managed service runs a standard component the provider maintains, and this database has no deployed application.

options.text: Yes — since the provider handles installation, patching and scaling, this meets the definition of PaaS regardless of what is deployed.
options.why: Provider-managed operations are common to both models; what makes PaaS specifically PaaS is the deployed application artifact, which is absent here.

options.text: No, because managed services are never provider-operated components, only self-hosted ones the customer configures remotely.
options.why: This gets the definition backwards — a managed service is precisely a provider-operated component; what stays with the customer is configuration, schema and data, not operation of the component itself.

options.text: Yes, because NIST SP 800-145 names managed services as a fourth service model alongside IaaS, PaaS and SaaS; NIST does not define managed services as a service model at all; it is a consumption pattern that fits within the same consumer/provider control split NIST documents for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
options.why: NIST does not define managed services as a service model at all; it is a consumption pattern that fits within the same consumer/provider control split NIST documents for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

items.rationale: Managed services and PaaS both take significant operational work off the customer, but PaaS is defined by the consumer deploying an application they wrote or acquired, while a managed service is a standard component — a database, queue or cache — the provider installs, patches and operates, that the consumer merely configures and uses through its ordinary interface. Nothing of the team's is deployed onto the database in this scenario, which settles it as a managed service.

items.stem: An application built on a managed database experiences repeated slow queries caused by a missing index. The team assumes the provider will fix it since the database is 'managed.' Is that assumption correct?

options.text: No — 'managed' takes over installation, patching, backup mechanics and failover, but schema design, indexes and query efficiency remain the customer's responsibility.
options.why: The guide names exactly this failure mode: a managed database still fails from a missing index, and none of that is the provider's to fix.

options.text: Yes — 'managed' means the provider assumes full responsibility for the database's behaviour, including the performance of queries and schema.
options.why: This is the misconception the guide corrects directly: managed does not mean no responsibility, and query and schema performance stay with whoever designed them.

options.text: Yes, because managed services provide the same automatic runtime optimisation PaaS platforms apply to deployed code.
options.why: PaaS platforms manage the runtime executing a deployed application; a managed database has no deployed application code to optimise, and query efficiency is a schema and query design concern the customer owns.

options.text: No, because this is actually a shared responsibility model failure specific to IaaS, not to managed services; IaaS is not involved here; the scenario is squarely about a managed database, where operational maintenance is the provider's and data-model decisions like indexing remain the customer's.
options.why: IaaS is not involved here; the scenario is squarely about a managed database, where operational maintenance is the provider's and data-model decisions like indexing remain the customer's.

items.rationale: A managed service trades configuration control for a large reduction in operational work, but it does not remove all responsibility: the provider installs, patches, backs up and monitors the component, while schema design, indexes, queries, data and access grants stay with the customer. A missing index causing slow queries is exactly the kind of failure the provider will not fix, because it is a decision the customer made, not an operational fault of the component.

items.stem: A provider deprecates the major version of a managed database a team has relied on for years, forcing an upgrade on a fixed timetable the team did not choose. Does this contradict the definition of a managed service?

options.text: No — losing control over the timing of a forced version upgrade is part of the trade a managed service makes; the customer keeps schema and data control but loses root and the ability to hold a retired version.
options.why: The guide states this precisely: providers apply updates in maintenance windows, and a version the provider deprecates forces an upgrade on their timetable, not the customer's.

options.text: Yes — a genuinely managed service never imposes an unplanned change, so version timing remains under the customer's control throughout.
options.why: This treats 'managed' as meaning 'never surprises you,' which the guide explicitly rejects — losing root and version-timing control is precisely what the customer trades away for reduced operational burden.

options.text: Yes, because forced runtime upgrades are a PaaS-specific behaviour that should never occur with a managed service; forced upgrades on the provider's schedule occur under both models for the same reason — the provider owns the underlying component's lifecycle in each case.
options.why: Forced upgrades on the provider's schedule occur under both models for the same reason — the provider owns the underlying component's lifecycle in each case.

options.text: No, but only because this database should have been run as IaaS instead, where version timing stays with the customer.
options.why: Running it as IaaS would indeed restore version-timing control, but that is a different architectural choice, not evidence about whether the forced upgrade contradicts the managed-service definition itself.

items.rationale: Trading configuration control for reduced operational burden is the definition of a managed service, and losing root — including the timing of forced version upgrades when the provider deprecates an old one — is exactly what that trade costs. It is not a contradiction of the definition; it is the definition working as intended, which is why the decision to accept a managed component should weigh that loss of control deliberately.

items.stem: Are actions taken through a cloud provider's web console audit-logged the same way as actions taken through its CLI or API?

options.text: Yes — on the major providers, console actions are logged by default alongside CLI, SDK and API actions; what the console lacks is a reviewable artifact, not an audit trail.
options.why: AWS CloudTrail explicitly records console actions alongside the CLI, SDKs and APIs, and equivalent logging exists on the other two major providers — the real gap is reproducibility, not auditability.

options.text: No — console actions leave no record at all, which is precisely why infrastructure as code is treated as the more auditable approach.
options.why: This is the routine misstatement the guide corrects: console work is recorded by default; what it lacks is an artifact you can review before it runs, re-run identically, or diff against last week.

options.text: Yes, but only if the customer explicitly enables logging for the console specifically; the major providers' baseline audit logging — CloudTrail's Event history, Azure's Activity Log, Google Cloud's Admin Activity logs — is available or always-on by default, not something the console specifically requires opting into.
options.why: The major providers' baseline audit logging — CloudTrail's Event history, Azure's Activity Log, Google Cloud's Admin Activity logs — is available or always-on by default, not something the console specifically requires opting into.

options.text: No, because only infrastructure-as-code changes are recorded as auditable events; all four interfaces are clients of the same API and are logged the same way; infrastructure as code's advantage is a declarative artifact to review, not exclusive access to audit logging.
options.why: All four interfaces are clients of the same API and are logged the same way; infrastructure as code's advantage is a declarative artifact to review, not exclusive access to audit logging.

items.rationale: AWS CloudTrail records actions taken by a user, role or service, explicitly including actions in the Management Console as well as the CLI, SDKs and APIs, with 90 days of Event history available automatically; Azure and Google Cloud provide equivalent always-on logging. Console work is therefore recorded — what it lacks is an artifact you can review before it runs, re-run identically, or diff against a prior state.

items.stem: A resource is deleted by hand through the web console, and a week later nobody can reconstruct exactly what state existed before the change or reproduce the fix reliably. What property of infrastructure as code, missing from the console, would have prevented this?

options.text: A declarative statement of desired state held in version control, reviewable before it is applied and comparable against reality so drift can be detected and corrected.
options.why: This is the property the guide names as what the other three interfaces lack: not an audit trail, but a versioned, comparable artifact of intended state.

options.text: Being audit-logged, since the console action itself left no record of who made the change; the console action would have been recorded by the provider's default audit logging just as thoroughly as a CLI or API call; the missing property is a reviewable, re-runnable artifact, not a log entry.
options.why: The console action would have been recorded by the provider's default audit logging just as thoroughly as a CLI or API call; the missing property is a reviewable, re-runnable artifact, not a log entry.

options.text: Being reachable over the network, since the console requires a browser session rather than a scriptable connection.
options.why: Network reachability is unrelated to the problem described; both the console and infrastructure as code operate over the network, and reachability was never in question.

options.text: Running under the shared responsibility model, which the console is exempt from; the shared responsibility model applies uniformly regardless of which interface makes a change; it has no bearing on whether a change is reviewable or reproducible.
options.why: The shared responsibility model applies uniformly regardless of which interface makes a change; it has no bearing on whether a change is reviewable or reproducible.

items.rationale: The CLI and API are imperative — a script states an action to take, not a state that should exist — so even they offer no guaranteed baseline to compare against. Infrastructure as code adds a declarative desired state held in version control: reviewable before applying, re-runnable identically, and comparable against live reality so that drift, including an unreviewed console deletion, can be detected and corrected.

items.stem: A single-instance application running in one availability zone goes down for forty minutes when that zone fails. The provider's platform-wide 99.99% SLA was still met for the month. Who is accountable for the outage, and what does the SLA actually hand the customer?

options.text: The customer's own architecture is accountable, since a single instance in one zone was exposed to that zone's failure; the SLA only prices the provider's own shortfall, not this outage.
options.why: The provider's SLA covers the platform, not the customer's placement decisions on top of it — availability at the customer's layer comes from their own redundancy design, exactly as the guide states.

options.text: The provider is accountable, since a 99.99% SLA is a guarantee that any application running on the platform will stay available, though availability at the customer's own layer is a design property no contract can substitute for.
options.why: An SLA is a contractual promise about the platform's own availability, not a guarantee about how a customer chooses to deploy on it; high availability is a design property the customer's own architecture must provide.

options.text: The provider is accountable, and the SLA entitles the customer to compensation for the business revenue the outage cost, though credits are typically capped well below what the outage actually cost the business.
options.why: SLA remedies are characteristically a service credit against future billing proportional to the shortfall, not compensation for the customer's business losses, and here the SLA threshold was not even missed.

options.text: The customer is accountable, but only because a managed database was involved in the outage rather than a compute instance.
options.why: The scenario describes a single compute instance failing with its zone; no managed database or its patching is implicated in why this outage occurred.

items.rationale: The provider's SLA is a promise about the platform, priced with a service credit if the provider's own threshold is missed — it says nothing about how a customer chooses to deploy on top of it. A single instance in one zone is exposed to exactly the kind of failure that redundancy across zones is meant to absorb; the SLA being met for the month changes nothing about that architectural gap, and the credit it would owe, if triggered at all, would be proportional to the provider's shortfall, not the customer's lost revenue.

items.stem: Google's SRE book gives a test for telling an SLA from an SLO. What is that test?

options.text: Ask what happens if the target is not met — if there is no explicit consequence, it is an SLO, not an SLA.
options.why: This is the SRE book's own stated test: an SLA is an explicit or implicit contract that includes consequences of meeting or missing the objectives it contains.

options.text: Ask whether the target is expressed as a percentage — a percentage always signals an SLA rather than an SLO; both SLAs and SLOs are commonly expressed as availability percentages; the numeric form tells you nothing about whether a consequence is attached.
options.why: Both SLAs and SLOs are commonly expressed as availability percentages; the numeric form tells you nothing about whether a consequence is attached.

options.text: Ask whether the target applies to the whole platform or to a single customer's account — platform-wide targets are SLAs, account-specific targets are SLOs.
options.why: Scope of application does not distinguish the two; an SLO can be platform-wide or team-specific, and what makes something an SLA is the presence of a contractual consequence, not its scope.

options.text: Ask whether the target is set by the provider or by the customer's own team — provider-set targets are SLAs, self-set targets are SLOs.
options.why: A provider can set internal SLOs of its own with no customer-facing consequence attached, so who sets the number does not settle whether it is an SLA.

items.rationale: The SRE book defines an SLA as an explicit or implicit contract with users that includes consequences of meeting or missing the objectives it contains, and offers exactly this diagnostic: ask what happens if the target is not met. If there is no explicit consequence, it is almost certainly an SLO being described, not an SLA.

items.stem: A team wants to put a transactional database's live data files directly on object storage to save on cost per gigabyte. Why does this fail mechanically rather than merely run slowly?

options.text: Object storage replaces an object as a whole on every write; a database needs random in-place writes at arbitrary offsets, which object storage has no mechanism for at all.
options.why: The guide states this precisely: whole-object replacement makes putting live database files there mechanically impossible, not merely slow.

options.text: Because object storage has a strict per-object size limit smaller than most database files; this object storage typically scales to enormous sizes; the actual blocker is the write model — whole-object replacement — not a size ceiling.
options.why: Object storage typically scales to enormous sizes; the actual blocker is the write model — whole-object replacement — not a size ceiling.

options.text: Because object storage cannot be reached over an HTTP API from the database engine; this object storage is specifically reached over an HTTP API; the mismatch is that a database needs partial, in-place writes, which that access model does not provide, not that it cannot be reached at all.
options.why: Object storage is specifically reached over an HTTP API; the mismatch is that a database needs partial, in-place writes, which that access model does not provide, not that it cannot be reached at all.

options.text: Because object storage requires a filesystem to be formatted onto it before use, unlike block storage; this reverses the two: block storage is what a guest OS formats with a filesystem; object storage has no filesystem to format at all, addressing items by key in a flat namespace instead.
options.why: This reverses the two: block storage is what a guest OS formats with a filesystem; object storage has no filesystem to format at all, addressing items by key in a flat namespace instead.

items.rationale: Object storage stores each item with its key and metadata, and a write replaces the whole object rather than editing bytes in place — there is no mechanism for a partial, in-place write at all. A database performs exactly that kind of random write to its data files, which is why object storage is not merely a slow choice for this use but a mechanically impossible one.

items.stem: Two application servers need to read and write the same set of files concurrently, with ordinary file permissions and locking. A second block storage volume is proposed for the second server. Why is that the wrong shape?

options.text: A block volume is normally attached to one instance at a time; sharing one between instances needs an explicit multi-attach feature plus a cluster-aware filesystem, which file storage over NFS or SMB provides natively.
options.why: The guide names this exact mismatch: block storage is not shared storage by default, and 'two servers need the same files' is a file-storage answer.

options.text: Object storage should be used instead, since it scales to any number of concurrent readers and writers; this object storage is not a mountable POSIX filesystem and has no partial-write or locking semantics; it is a poor fit for files two servers actively edit together, unlike file storage.
options.why: Object storage is not a mountable POSIX filesystem and has no partial-write or locking semantics; it is a poor fit for files two servers actively edit together, unlike file storage.

options.text: A second block volume works fine, because block storage automatically synchronises writes between any volumes attached to the same account.
options.why: Block volumes have no built-in cross-volume synchronisation; each is an independent raw device unless deliberately mirrored, which does not solve concurrent shared access at all.

options.text: A second block volume works fine, provided both servers are in the same availability zone; this zone placement does not change the fact that a block volume is normally attached to a single instance at a time; proximity does not enable concurrent shared attachment on its own.
options.why: Zone placement does not change the fact that a block volume is normally attached to a single instance at a time; proximity does not enable concurrent shared attachment on its own.

items.rationale: Block storage exposes a raw volume that a guest OS formats and normally attaches to a single instance at a time — sharing it needs an explicit multi-attach feature and a cluster-aware filesystem most teams do not have set up. File storage puts the filesystem on the provider's side and serves it over NFS or SMB precisely so that many machines can mount the same tree concurrently with familiar permissions and locking, which is exactly this requirement.

items.stem: In object storage, is a 'folder' shown in a console listing a real directory?

options.text: No — it is a prefix on the object's key; the namespace is flat and has no real directory structure underneath it.
options.why: The guide states this directly: what looks like a folder in object storage is a prefix on the key, not an actual directory.

items.stem: AWS's prescriptive guidance names seven migration strategies, the '7 Rs.' Which term does AWS actually use for replacing an application with a different product, typically SaaS, rather than migrating the existing one?

options.text: Repurchase — also called drop and shop.
options.why: AWS's own term is repurchase; the guide flags this specifically because the term is easy to misremember as 'replace.'

options.text: Replace — the customer swaps the application for a different product entirely, though 'replace' is not one of AWS's seven; the correct term for this strategy is repurchase.
options.why: 'Replace' is not one of AWS's seven; the correct term for this strategy is repurchase, and this project has gotten that substitution wrong before.

options.text: Relocate — the workload moves to the cloud without changing its architecture; this relocate specifically leaves the application's architecture untouched; it does not involve swapping the application for a different product.
options.why: Relocate specifically leaves the application's architecture untouched; it does not involve swapping the application for a different product.

options.text: Refactor — the application is rebuilt around cloud-native patterns; this refactor rebuilds the existing application for the cloud; it does not describe dropping the application in favour of a different product.
options.why: Refactor rebuilds the existing application for the cloud; it does not describe dropping the application in favour of a different product.

items.rationale: AWS's prescriptive guidance names the seven strategies as retire, retain, rehost, relocate, repurchase, replatform, and refactor or re-architect. Repurchase — sometimes called drop and shop — is specifically the strategy of replacing an application with a different product or version, typically SaaS; 'replace' is not the term AWS uses, and this guide corrects that exact error.

items.stem: A large migration programme deliberately avoids refactoring any application during the move itself, planning to modernise afterward instead. Which strategies does AWS recommend favouring during the migration, and why not refactor now?

options.text: Rehost, replatform, relocate and retire are the common strategies for large migrations; refactoring during the move is the most complex and costly strategy and is hard to manage across many applications at once.
options.why: This matches AWS's own guidance directly: modernise after the move, not during it, because refactoring while migrating compounds the complexity of both efforts at once.

options.text: Repurchase alone should be used for every application, since it is the fastest of the seven strategies; AWS names relocate, not repurchase, as the quickest strategy, and using one strategy for every application ignores that each workload is assessed and assigned individually.
options.why: AWS names relocate, not repurchase, as the quickest strategy, and using one strategy for every application ignores that each workload is assessed and assigned individually.

options.text: Refactor should still be used first, since it is the strategy AWS calls the quickest way to migrate and operate in the cloud.
options.why: AWS reserves 'quickest' for relocate specifically, because it leaves the application's architecture untouched; refactor is the strategy AWS calls the most complex and costly, the opposite of quick.

options.text: Retain and retire should never appear in a large migration plan, since every application must eventually move to the cloud.
options.why: AWS lists retire and retain as legitimate strategies in their own right; a portfolio assessment that retires an unused application or retains one with a hardware dependency avoids unnecessary migration cost entirely.

items.rationale: AWS notes that common strategies for large migrations are rehost, replatform, relocate and retire, and recommends against refactoring during the migration itself, since modernising while moving is the most complex option and hard to manage across many applications — the recommended sequence is to migrate cheaply first with one of the low-effort strategies, then modernise afterward once the workload is safely running in the cloud.

items.stem: What accumulates to create vendor lock-in?

options.text: Dependence on provider-specific services and interfaces, the volume of data and its egress charges, and the team's operational knowledge and tooling built around one platform.
options.why: These are the three sources the guide names together as accumulating into the cost of leaving a provider.

options.text: Lock-in is a defect that well-run cloud architecture avoids entirely, so choosing a provider-specific managed service is always an architectural mistake.
options.why: The guide frames lock-in as a trade-off to price, not a defect to eliminate — provider-specific services are often chosen precisely because they genuinely reduce work.

options.text: Only the technical portability of the application code, since data and team expertise are irrelevant to switching providers.
options.why: Portable code reduces only the technical component of lock-in; data gravity, egress cost and accumulated team expertise remain untouched by code portability alone.

options.text: The length of the provider's published SLA, since a longer SLA commits a customer for longer; an SLA is a contractual availability commitment with a remedy for shortfalls; it has no bearing on how costly it would be to move a workload to a different provider.
options.why: An SLA is a contractual availability commitment with a remedy for shortfalls; it has no bearing on how costly it would be to move a workload to a different provider.

items.rationale: Lock-in comes from three accumulating sources: depending on provider-specific services and interfaces, the sheer volume of data that would need to move plus the egress charges for moving it, and the operational knowledge and tooling a team has built around one platform. None of these is eliminated by addressing only one of the three.

items.stem: A team adopts containers, an orchestrator and standard SQL specifically to reduce lock-in before choosing a cloud provider. Does this eliminate their exposure to vendor lock-in?

options.text: No — these portability layers reduce the technical component of lock-in, but they do not touch data gravity, egress cost, or the operational expertise the team will still build up around whichever provider it chooses.
options.why: The guide states this directly: portable layers reduce technical portability barriers but leave the other sources of lock-in untouched.

options.text: Yes — using only portable, standard technologies removes vendor lock-in entirely, regardless of provider; this overstates what portability buys; even with fully portable code, the data itself and the team's accumulated platform-specific knowledge still create real costs of leaving.
options.why: This overstates what portability buys; even with fully portable code, the data itself and the team's accumulated platform-specific knowledge still create real costs of leaving.

options.text: Yes, because containers and standard SQL guarantee the application can be moved back to on-premises hardware at no cost.
options.why: Moving back to on-premises would still involve the same data-volume, egress and re-tooling costs the guide describes; portability lowers the technical barrier, not the cost to zero.

options.text: No, because standard SQL only works with a single specific cloud provider's managed database offering; this standard SQL is deliberately provider-neutral; the actual limitation is that portability layers do not address data gravity or accumulated expertise, not that standard SQL is somehow tied to one vendor.
options.why: Standard SQL is deliberately provider-neutral; the actual limitation is that portability layers do not address data gravity or accumulated expertise, not that standard SQL is somehow tied to one vendor.

items.rationale: Portable layers — containers, an orchestrator, standard SQL, open protocols, declarative infrastructure — reduce the technical component of lock-in by keeping the application itself movable. They do nothing, however, about data gravity, the egress cost of actually moving stored data, or the operational expertise a team accumulates around whichever platform it operates day to day, so choosing portable technology narrows lock-in without eliminating it.
